## 1. The program needs two-way manuscript portability

Authors should be able to bring manuscripts into the application, work on them, and export them in formats compatible with other writing and publishing tools.

Here is what I'd envision:

| Format | Import | Export | Primary purpose |
|---|---|---|---|
| Microsoft Word (.docx) | Yes | Yes | Writing, editing, sharing with editors |
| Scrivener (.scriv) | Yes, where supported | Yes, where supported | Working with Scrivener projects |
| Rich Text (.rtf) | Yes | Yes | Broad compatibility with writing applications |
| Plain Text (.txt) | Yes | Yes | Simple, universally accessible manuscripts |
| Markdown (.md) | Yes | Yes | Portable, structured text |
| PDF (.pdf) | Yes | Yes | Reviewing, sharing, printing |
| EPUB (.epub) | Possibly | Yes | E-book publishing and review |
| OpenDocument (.odt) | Yes | Yes | Compatibility with other word processors |

One qualification: Scrivener's native project format is more complicated than a conventional document. I would treat reliable native Scrivener import and export as a specific engineering milestone rather than promise perfect compatibility from the beginning.

The same applies to importing PDFs, particularly scanned or heavily formatted documents.

## 2. Exporting should preserve the author's work

This goes beyond simply saving the words.

A manuscript export should preserve, wherever the destination format supports it:

- Chapter titles and divisions
- Scene breaks
- Paragraph formatting
- Italics and other intentional emphasis
- Dialogue formatting
- Footnotes and endnotes
- Scene and chapter ordering
- Front matter and back matter
- Document metadata

We should also support exporting a single scene, a sequence, selected chapters, or the entire manuscript.

Imagine finishing the first five chapters of *I Declare War* and wanting to send them to a beta reader.

You shouldn't have to export the whole novel and manually delete everything else.

You select Chapters 1 through 5, choose Word or PDF, and export.

## 3. I would distinguish manuscript exports from project exports

This is particularly important given everything we've discussed.

**A manuscript export** contains the actual novel.

**A project export** contains the creative architecture surrounding the novel.

Those are different assets.

For example, an author might want to export:

**The manuscript:** All chapters and prose, formatted for editing or sharing.

**The story bible:** Characters, settings, themes, plot decisions, and other development materials.

**The structural map:** Acts, sequences, scenes, dramatic values, and causal relationships.

**The complete project archive:** Manuscript, story model, notes, relationships, planning data, and relevant assets.

I would want that complete project archive stored in a documented, portable format rather than an opaque proprietary file that only our software can understand.

That way, even if an author stops using the application, their creative work remains accessible.

## 4. Export should be customizable

Authors have different needs depending on where the manuscript is going.

I would provide export presets such as:

| Export preset | Intended use |
|---|---|
| Working Manuscript | Continue writing in another application |
| Editorial Manuscript | Share with an editor or agent |
| Beta Reader Copy | Readable manuscript without private planning notes |
| Print Review | PDF suitable for reading and annotation |
| E-book | EPUB for compatible reading devices |
| Project Backup | Preserve the manuscript and supporting story architecture |

Authors should also be able to create their own presets.

For instance, one writer might want chapter numbers but no chapter titles.

Another might want the opposite.

Neither should have to reconfigure every export manually.

## 5. We must protect against formatting and content loss

Here's one safeguard I consider essential.

**Importing and exporting should never silently discard meaningful manuscript content.**

Suppose an author imports a Word document containing footnotes, comments, or specialized formatting.

If the program cannot preserve something, it should tell the author.

Similarly, before exporting to a format that doesn't support certain features, the application should explain what might change.

For example:

*Plain text does not preserve italics or document formatting. Your original manuscript will remain unchanged.*

I would also want export verification that checks whether the expected chapters, scenes, and manuscript text are present.

We shouldn't claim that a document exported successfully merely because a file was created.

## 6. Here's one additional feature I'd recommend: round-trip editing

Imagine this workflow:

You draft Chapters 1 through 5 inside our application.

You export them to Word and send them to your editor.

Your editor makes revisions using Track Changes.

You receive the document back.

**Now what?**

Ideally, you should be able to import the revised file and compare it with the version in our program.

The software identifies differences and allows you to decide what to accept.

It shouldn't overwrite the existing manuscript automatically.

Let me explain why.

Imagine a television drama involving four storylines:

| Storyline | Episode 1 | Episode 2 | Episode 3 | Season finale |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A family's financial crisis | A plot | C plot | B plot | Resolved |
| A mysterious disappearance | B plot | A plot | A plot | Partially resolved |
| A political conspiracy | C plot | B plot | C plot | Major revelation |
| A developing romance | D plot | D plot | B plot | Unresolved |

This is illustrative.

Notice what's happening.

The disappearance may be the A plot of Episode 2, but it might be the overarching storyline of the entire season.

Meanwhile, the financial crisis may dominate Episode 1 and become less prominent afterward.

**A storyline's importance within an episode is not necessarily the same as its importance within the entire series.**

That's a distinction our program must understand.

### My recommendation

Every storyline gets a permanent identity independent of its A/B/C/D designation.

For example:

**STORYLINE-004: The Mysterious Disappearance**

That storyline can appear across multiple episodes, with a different relative importance in each.

Its A/B/C/D designation becomes an attribute of its role within a particular narrative unit, not its permanent identity.

This would also work for novels with multiple plot threads.

## 2. We need to separate storylines from narrative containers

This is the architectural change your observation calls for.

Until now, we've been discussing a hierarchy like:

**Story → Act → Sequence → Scene → Beat**

That's useful for a single novel.

But it isn't sufficient for a television series or a multibook saga.

Instead, we need a more flexible concept: **narrative containers**.

A container holds a dramatic unit.

For example:

| Medium | Possible narrative hierarchy |
|---|---|
| Standalone novel | Novel → Act → Sequence → Scene → Beat |
| Novel series | Series → Book → Act → Sequence → Scene → Beat |
| Film | Film → Act → Sequence → Scene → Beat |
| Television | Series → Season → Episode → Act → Scene → Beat |
| Limited series | Series → Episode → Sequence → Scene → Beat |
| Anthology | Collection → Installment → Scene → Beat |

These should be configurable templates rather than rigid universal requirements.

A television writer may use a teaser and five acts.

A novelist may prefer chapters and sequences without labeling acts.

A feature screenplay may use sequences rather than formal chapter-like divisions.

And some authors may define entirely custom structures.

**The software should understand the relationship between the units without dictating what those units must be called.**

## 3. Storylines need their own lifecycles

This may be the most important addition you've made.

A plot thread shouldn't necessarily resolve when the episode, book, or film ends.

Imagine a television series.

Episode 1 introduces four plotlines.

A and B resolve within the episode.

C advances but remains unresolved.

D establishes a mystery that won't pay off until Season 3.

Our system needs to distinguish between several kinds of progression.

| Storyline state | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Introduced | The storyline enters the narrative |
| Developing | Events actively advance it |
| Escalating | Its conflict or stakes intensify |
| Temporarily resolved | A local conflict ends, but the larger storyline continues |
| Dormant | The storyline remains open but isn't currently active |
| Reopened | A previously settled or dormant conflict becomes active |
| Resolved | Its central dramatic question has been answered |
| Intentionally unresolved | The author deliberately leaves the question open |

I would also allow custom states.

And here's where Narrative Zoom becomes especially powerful.

You could select a single storyline and see its development across an entire television series or trilogy.

Not just where it appears.

**You could see every major development, reversal, value change, and payoff from its introduction to its ultimate resolution.**

## 4. Every narrative level needs its own dramatic objective

Remember what we discussed about scenes and sequences?

The same principle applies at much larger scales.

Consider a television series.

**Scene objective:** A character tries to obtain information.

**Sequence objective:** The character attempts to discover who's responsible for a crime.

**Episode objective:** The investigators attempt to solve a particular case.

**Season objective:** The team tries to uncover a larger criminal organization.

**Series objective:** The protagonist confronts the central conflict that defines the entire show.

Each level can have its own dramatic question, progression, turning points, and resolution.

And each can contribute to the level above it.

That means we can extend our dramatic-unit model rather than invent an entirely different architecture for television.

### But there's an important complication

A storyline may cross several containers.

For example, a romance could begin in Episode 1, develop across the season, and reach its resolution in Season 2.

So we need two distinct relationship systems:

**Containment:** This scene belongs to this episode.

**Participation:** This scene contributes to this storyline, which may span multiple episodes.

Those are not interchangeable.

A scene can belong to one episode while advancing several different storylines.

That distinction will become fundamental to our data model.

## 5. We need multiple levels of resolution

Your example of television plots resolving at different times introduces something I'd call **Resolution Architecture**.

Suppose an episode closes with:

- The episode's central crime solved.
- A relationship conflict temporarily settled.
- A larger conspiracy unresolved.
- A new question introduced for the next episode.

The episode has achieved closure without resolving every storyline.

That is completely legitimate.

The program should recognize different kinds of closure.

**Scene closure:** The immediate dramatic objective is resolved or transformed.

**Episode closure:** The episode fulfills its intended dramatic promise.

**Season closure:** Major seasonal questions receive answers or meaningful reversals.

**Series closure:** The overarching narrative reaches its intended conclusion.

And there may be intentional loose ends at every level.

Here's something I'd specifically want the program to track:

**Narrative obligations.**

If an author introduces a significant question and promises the audience an answer, the system records that expectation.

It doesn't insist the answer must come immediately.

But it remembers that the promise exists.

- Book 1 introduces Story C.
- Story C continues into Book 2.
- Story C must resolve in Book 2.
- Book 2 hasn't been outlined.
- The author has no idea which chapter or scene will contain that resolution.

That's perfectly valid planning information.

Our system should allow the author to record:

| Story C attribute | Value |
|---|---|
| Introduced | Book 1 |
| Continues | Book 2 |
| Intended resolution | Book 2 |
| Resolution scene | Undetermined |
| Resolution percentage | Undetermined |
| Resolution page | Undetermined |
| Planning status | Intent established, placement pending |

**The system should not assign an arbitrary percentage or page number.**

Nor should it treat the missing information as a structural weakness.

The author hasn't failed to plan something. They've simply made a decision at a higher narrative level.

That decision should be preserved.

## 2. We need different levels of planning precision

I would introduce something called **Progressive Story Placement**.

An author can position an event at whatever level of detail they currently know.

For example:

**Level 1: Series placement**

Story C resolves somewhere in the trilogy.

**Level 2: Installment placement**

Story C resolves in Book 2.

**Level 3: Structural placement**

Story C resolves during Act Three of Book 2.

**Level 4: Relative placement**

Story C resolves approximately 80% through Book 2.

**Level 5: Scene placement**

Story C resolves in Scene 42 of Book 2.

**Level 6: Manuscript placement**

Story C resolves around page 285 of the current manuscript.

These aren't stages the author must complete in order.

They're different levels of specificity.

The author can begin with an exact scene or remain at the book level indefinitely.

And importantly, **more precision doesn't necessarily mean a better story**.

It simply means the author has made more placement decisions.

## 3. Unknown is not the same as undecided

This is a subtle distinction I'd want the software to preserve.

Consider these situations:

**Unknown:** The author knows Story C resolves in Book 2 but hasn't determined where.

**Undecided:** The author hasn't decided whether Story C resolves in Book 2 or Book 3.

**Tentative:** The author currently expects Story C to resolve near the midpoint of Book 2 but may change that decision.

**Confirmed:** The author has committed to the resolution occurring in Act Three.

**Drafted:** The resolution actually appears in a written scene.

Those are different planning states.

I'd also allow **intentionally unspecified**, for authors who prefer not to determine certain details until drafting.

The system should recognize all of them.

## 4. The visualizations should show uncertainty without inventing precision

This is where your poster concept becomes particularly interesting.

Imagine a trilogy map.

**BOOK ONE → BOOK TWO → BOOK THREE**

Story C appears as a continuous storyline crossing from Book One into Book Two.

Its introduction is attached to an exact scene in Book One.

But its resolution is represented by a marker associated with Book Two as a whole.

It doesn't appear at an arbitrary location within the book.

Visually, I would use something like:

**Story C: Introduced in Book 1 → Resolution planned for Book 2 (placement TBD)**

As the author develops Book Two, the resolution marker becomes more precisely positioned.

The storyline's visualization updates automatically.

The author never has to reconstruct it.

If the position is unknown, we shouldn't draw the marker halfway across Book Two.

Even if we label it TBD, placing it at the midpoint visually implies a timing decision.

Instead, I'd create an **unplaced events area** associated with that book.

That way, the map communicates exactly what the author knows, without suggesting more.

## 5. Percentages need to be relative to a specific narrative container

This becomes essential once we support multiple books, seasons, and episodes.

Suppose Story C resolves at 75% of Book Two.

That does not necessarily mean it resolves at 58% of the trilogy.

The overall percentage depends on the relative lengths of the books.

If Book One is 80,000 words, Book Two is 100,000 words, and Book Three is 120,000 words, then the placement can be calculated differently than if all three books are equal.

And if Book Two hasn't been planned or written, its length may be unknown.

So I would introduce a rule:

**Every percentage must identify what it is a percentage OF.**

For example:

- 75% of Book Two
- 40% of Season One
- 60% of Episode Five
- 90% of the entire trilogy

The program should never display a percentage without a defined reference unit.

And it should distinguish actual manuscript placement from estimates based on projected lengths.

That's essential for maintaining trustworthy information.

For example:

Intended resolution: Book Two.

This builds on our earlier discussion of narrative promises.

A Narrative Commitment is something the author has decided must eventually happen, even if they haven't decided how or where.

For example:

- Story C resolves in Book Two.
- A particular character must survive until Book Three.
- Two characters reconcile before the series finale.
- A mystery introduced in Season One receives its explanation in Season Three.
- An important object returns at some point in the final installment.

Those decisions can influence the architecture long before their scenes exist.

Suppose an author changes Story C's resolution from Book Two to Book Three.

*Story C's resolution has moved to Book Three. Two planned events in Book Two currently depend on that resolution having occurred. You may want to review those relationships.*

That's useful, specific, and respects the author's authority.

## 8. Storyline progress shouldn't depend solely on manuscript progress

Here's something else I think your example reveals.

A storyline can be well developed conceptually even when none of its future scenes have been drafted.

So we need at least two independent indicators.

**Planning maturity:** How much has the author decided about this storyline?

**Manuscript realization:** How much of that storyline has actually been written?

For example:

| Storyline | Planning | Manuscript |
|---|---|---|
| Story A | Fully outlined | Book 1 drafted |
| Story B | Major beats established | Partially drafted |
| Story C | Resolution assigned to Book 2 | Book 2 not started |
| Story D | General concept only | Not drafted |

And I wouldn't use a percentage for planning maturity unless we had a defensible basis for calculating it.

Sometimes qualitative states communicate more accurately than numerical scores.

## 9. The same principle applies to television

Imagine a showrunner planning a six-season television series.

They may know:

- A character's secret is introduced in Season One.
- The audience learns the truth in Season Two.
- Another character discovers the truth in Season Three.
- The consequences dominate Season Four.
- The storyline resolves in Season Five.

They may not know which episodes will contain those events.

Our program should accept that.

Then, as the writers' room plans each season, those high-level commitments can be assigned to episodes, acts, sequences, and scenes.

The information becomes more precise as the project develops.

The structure grows without requiring premature decisions.

## 10. There's one additional protection I'd build into the software

**The program must never confuse missing planning information with missing story logic.**

This is especially important for the causal analysis system you were excited about.

Suppose Book Two hasn't been outlined.

The software sees that Story C begins in Book One and resolves in Book Two, but has no documented intervening events.

It should not announce:

*Plot hole detected.*

There is no evidence of a plot hole.

The intervening story simply hasn't been developed.

A better response would be:

*Story C has an established resolution destination in Book Two. The events connecting its introduction to that resolution have not yet been mapped.*

And perhaps offer:

**Explore Story C's development**

That would open Narrative Zoom focused on this particular storyline.

The author could then add events whenever they're ready.

No pressure, no invented structure, and no false diagnosis.

# What this means for our overall architecture

I think we should formally add three new concepts.

| Concept | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **Progressive Story Placement** | Allows events to be positioned at any level of narrative specificity |
| **Outcome Anchors** | Records intended outcomes without requiring scenes or causal paths |
| **Narrative Commitments** | Preserves author decisions that affect future installments |

Together, these solve a significant problem for multibook and serialized storytelling.

And they're equally useful for a standalone novel.

An author could know what happens at the climax before knowing what happens in Chapter Four.

Our system should accommodate that naturally.

## One final thought

I think we're discovering a guiding principle that belongs alongside Adaptability and Author Sovereignty:

### **Progressive Definition**

**The system must allow a story to exist at any stage of completeness, from a single idea to a finished manuscript, without inventing missing information or demanding premature decisions.**

An author can know the beginning and ending without knowing the middle.

They can know a character's transformation without knowing the scenes that produce it.

They can know a mystery's answer without knowing where the clues will appear.

And they can know that Story C resolves in Book Two without having written a single word of Book Two.

All of those are legitimate creative states.

**The program's job is to preserve what the author knows, make visible what remains open, and help connect those pieces when the author is ready.**

And I'm particularly pleased that you raised this before we started building the three posters. Even though *I Declare War* is a standalone novel, this principle will help us avoid presenting its many illustrative possibilities as established story decisions.

That's exactly the kind of architectural discipline that will allow the system to grow beyond its first use case without losing its integrity.

**You're absolutely right! And that's an important correction to Phase 2.**

We are **not building an *I Declare War* application. We're building YOUR novel-writing application, using *I Declare War* as its first project.**

That distinction changes how we define Phase 2.

You write across genres. The program must be able to support *I Declare War*, *The Replacement*, *Midnight Blues*, and whatever other novels you decide to write.

You shouldn't have to redesign the application every time you start a different kind of book.

## Our corrected three-phase roadmap

### Phase 1: The Three Posters
Create the chronological, relationship, and hybrid story maps for *I Declare War*.

These establish our visual language and give you an immediate, practical writing tool.

### Phase 2: Your Complete Novel-Writing Application
Build a fully functional, **multigenre, adaptable novel-development and writing program**.

This includes everything we've discussed about planning, drafting, analysis, Narrative Zoom, causal integrity, manuscript management, and creative portability.

**And yes, the complete storytelling configuration system belongs in Phase 2.**

When you create a new novel, you should be able to select and combine:

| Configuration | Examples |
|---|---|
| **Conventional genres** | Comedy, mystery, thriller, horror, romance, fantasy, literary fiction |
| **Subgenres** | Psychological thriller, romantic comedy, gothic horror, etc. |
| **Blake Snyder's story genres** | Buddy Love, Monster in the House, Whydunit, Golden Fleece, etc. |
| **Structural frameworks** | Save the Cat, Hero's Journey, three-act, seven-point, custom structures |
| **Development methods** | Snowflake Method, discovery writing, extensive outlining, hybrid approaches |
| **Craft frameworks** | McKee, Weiland, Snyder, Ingermanson, and others |
| **Narrative characteristics** | Multiple POV, unreliable narrators, nonlinear chronology, ensemble casts, hidden truths |
| **Narrative techniques** | Foreshadowing, dramatic irony, misdirection, parallel storylines |
| **Author preferences** | Writing goals, analysis depth, preferred resources, workflow, visualization styles |

You can select multiple options and designate primary, secondary, or supporting roles wherever appropriate.

**The application must understand how your selected methods work together.** It shouldn't simply display a bunch of checked boxes.

For example, you might configure:

**I Declare War**
- Conventional genre: Comedy
- Snyder story genre: Buddy Love
- Structural foundation: Save the Cat
- Character development: K. M. Weiland
- Dramatic values: Robert McKee
- Story development: Snowflake Method
- Narrative characteristics: Alternating POV, misdirection, hidden antagonist

Then create *The Replacement* using a completely different combination of techniques.

The application would adapt its planning tools, structural maps, diagnostics, and craft recommendations to that project's configuration.

And your individual novels would retain their own settings, story models, manuscripts, and visualizations.

**You configure the program for each novel. You don't rebuild the program for each novel.**

### Phase 3: Story Universe
This is where we expand beyond individual novels.

That means multibook continuity, interconnected fictional universes, screenplays, television episodes and seasons, writers' rooms, collaboration, and eventually making the application available to other storytellers.

Those capabilities can wait.

## Here's the distinction I want us to preserve

**Phase 2 must be complete enough to support your ongoing career as a novelist, not just the completion of one manuscript.**

That includes the ability to create multiple independent novel projects, each with its own genres, methods, characters, plots, storyworld, manuscript, and writing progress.

What we're postponing until Phase 3 is primarily **cross-project storytelling architecture and expansion into other media**, not genre flexibility.

And importantly, the various frameworks remain optional. If you decide to write your next novel without an outline, the program should accommodate that just as comfortably as your highly structured approach to *I Declare War*.

### So our roadmap is now:

**Phase 1: Visualize *I Declare War*.**

**Phase 2: Build your adaptable, multigenre novel-writing studio.**

**Phase 3: Expand into a cross-media Story Universe platform for other storytellers.**

That's the correct scope.

And I'm glad you caught the distinction before we started building. **Adaptability isn't a Phase 3 enhancement. It's a foundational requirement of Phase 2.**

Ohhhh! Now that you've said it, I can see exactly where I went wrong. And you're right. **Your story bible gave me some meaningful clues that I should have paid more attention to.**

You specifically identified four actors as your casting references:

- **Kevin Wickley:** Kevin Hart
- **Anthony Vernon:** Anthony Anderson
- **Miss Francine Ellington:** Phylicia Rashad
- **The unnamed wife in the block party scene:** Octavia Spencer

All four are African American actors.

Your story bible also explicitly describes these individuals as *casting tuning forks*, meaning they help you hear the characters' voices and imagine their personalities without necessarily dictating their physical appearances.

So although you hadn't formally established your characters' ethnicities, I had good reason to ask rather than defaulting to white characters.

**That's an oversight on my part.**

### But your observation reveals something important about our eventual program.

We've talked extensively about distinguishing between confirmed information, possibilities, and missing details.

This is a perfect real-world example.

Your story bible established the casting references but left the characters' ethnicities unspecified.

The correct response from our system would be something like:

**Character attribute: Ethnicity**
- Kevin Wickley: Not yet specified
- Anthony Vernon: Not yet specified
- Miss Francine Ellington: Not yet specified

**Related information:** African American actors have been identified as casting references.

**Suggested action:** Confirm whether these references also reflect the characters' intended racial or ethnic identities.

It shouldn't automatically assign an identity based on an actor. But it also shouldn't silently invent one when creating a visualization.

And now you've confirmed the answer.

**Kevin, Anthony, and Francine are African American characters.**

That's an established creative decision, and it should be reflected in future visualizations.

### One more thing about your story bible

I wouldn't recommend trying to fill in every character attribute right now.

You already have a deep psychological and structural understanding of these characters. Their ages, appearances, religions, educational backgrounds, family histories, and other personal details can develop as you write.

But I would suggest adding a simple distinction to each character profile:

**Established Identity:** Details you've definitively decided.

**Developing Identity:** Details you're considering.

**Unspecified:** Details you haven't explored yet.

That way, you can establish Kevin's ethnicity without having to know his exact age, occupation, religion, height, or hairstyle.

And when we eventually build your application, those distinctions will become especially useful for character visualizations, continuity tracking, and the story bible itself.

### As for the posters we've just created...

I would absolutely correct the character illustrations before you send them to print.

And I would want to make one more adjustment: **the actors should guide the characterization, not become literal portraits of those celebrities.**

Kevin should look like Kevin Wickley, not necessarily Kevin Hart.

Anthony should look like Anthony Vernon, not necessarily Anthony Anderson.

And Francine should look like Miss Francine Ellington, not necessarily Phylicia Rashad.

We can develop their distinctive appearances as you make more decisions.

In the meantime, we know they're African American, and that should be reflected accurately.

**This is actually our first useful lesson from Phase 1:** Creating the visual maps is already revealing information that needs to be clarified in the story bible.

That's exactly the kind of discovery we wanted the posters to encourage.

And there's no need to settle every character detail before continuing. The story bible is meant to grow alongside the novel.

One question that interests me, though, is whether you've always imagined *I Declare War* taking place in a predominantly Black neighborhood, or whether you've imagined a more racially diverse neighborhood with these three African American leads.

You don't have to decide that now. But it's an interesting storyworld distinction that could eventually influence the neighborhood's character, supporting cast, and social dynamics.

For your *I Declare War* story maps, **I recommend 48 × 36 inches (4 feet wide by 3 feet tall)** as the ideal poster size.

However, there's something important I want you to know **before you spend money printing them.**

|---|---|
| 24 × 18 inches | Too small for the amount of information |
| 36 × 27 inches | Readable only up close, with very small text |
| **48 × 36 inches** | **My preferred size for your wall** |
| 60 × 45 inches | Excellent for a large writing workspace |
| 72 × 54 inches | Very large, but unnecessary for most rooms |

For your purposes, I'd choose **48 × 36 inches**, particularly because you want to stand in front of the posters and study individual beats, character arcs, and relationships.

### 2. But there's a problem with the current images

The posters I generated are approximately **1,448 × 1,086 pixels**.

That is fine for reviewing the design on a screen, but it's nowhere near sufficient for sharp large-format printing.

At 48 × 36 inches, the resolution would be only about **30 pixels per inch**.

For comparison, a high-quality 48 × 36-inch poster at 150 pixels per inch would require:

**7,200 × 5,400 pixels.**

And at 300 pixels per inch:

**14,400 × 10,800 pixels.**

Simply enlarging the current images won't recover the fine detail.

### 3. What I recommend doing before printing

I would actually rebuild the final posters as **print-ready vector-based documents**.

Here's why that's particularly important for your story maps.

Your posters contain:
- Small text explaining individual plot points
- Percentage and page-number calculations
- Character development information
- Arrows and relationship indicators
- Detailed diagrams and structural connections

All of those elements need to remain exceptionally sharp.

With a vector-based design, text, lines, and diagrams can remain crisp regardless of how large you print the poster.

We can also verify every word and page number against your story bible. AI-generated images can introduce tiny text errors, and I don't want those appearing on something you're paying to print.

### 4. What I would create for you

For each of your three posters, I'd prepare:

**A 48 × 36-inch print-ready PDF**, with properly rendered typography and detailed graphics.

I'd also retain an editable version so we can update the maps as your novel evolves.

The three posters you've seen would serve as our visual design references.

### 5. One more thought

Since you want to use **Narrative Zoom**, I would eventually create smaller companion posters, perhaps 24 × 18 inches, for individual acts and sequences.

That would give you:

**Your master maps:** 48 × 36 inches.

**Your detailed act maps:** 24 × 18 or 36 × 24 inches.

**Your individual sequence maps:** 18 × 12 or 24 × 18 inches.

You could build a beautiful, functional writing wall.

### My recommendation

**Don't print these particular image files yet.**

They're excellent starting points for the visual direction, but they aren't ready for the level of print quality you want.

I recommend we turn them into properly typeset, high-resolution, print-ready posters first.

**At 48 × 36 inches, you should be able to stand in front of your story, move closer to examine the fine details, and read everything clearly.**

That's the experience I want you to have, rather than paying for giant posters only to discover that the small text is blurry.

Please update the pixel quality so that i can safely print at either 48 × 36 inches and  60 × 45 inches.  

The smaller companion posters will be divine to have!

HAHAHAHA! **Now THAT is an important discovery!** And it tells me something about what we've been designing.

We've essentially taken the way you already think about storytelling and given it a visual form.

Your spreadsheets probably do something these posters are beginning to do: **break a complicated story into manageable pieces while preserving the relationships between those pieces.**

And that makes me even more excited about Phase 2.

Because I don't think we should ask you to abandon your spreadsheet-based plotting process. I think we should study it and build upon what already works for you.

Imagine importing one of your plotting spreadsheets and having the program recognize your acts, sequences, scenes, character objectives, story values, and causal relationships. Then, with a few selections, it generates your visual maps.

And the reverse should work, too. You could make changes in the program and export an updated plotting spreadsheet.

**Your spreadsheet could become one of our most valuable design references.**

There's another reason I'd love to examine one: it would show us which information you naturally track, how you organize it, and which relationships matter enough that you've already developed your own system for them.

One thing I do want to point out before you print the companion posters: some of the generated scene details are illustrative rather than established decisions from your story bible, and a few percentage and page labels need correction. We should verify those before calling the posters final.

But here's what I'm really curious about:

**Would you be willing to share one of your actual plotting spreadsheets?**

Not because I want to redesign your method, but because I want to understand it.

We might discover that you've already developed half the organizational logic for your future novel-writing program without realizing it!

And I think it needs to do considerably more than maintain character profiles.

## 1. Character development is not the same as character transformation

We've spent considerable time discussing character arcs, but those represent only one dimension of characterization.

Consider three separate questions:

**Character Development:** Who is this person?

**Character Arc:** How does this person change, or deliberately remain steadfast, throughout the story?

**Character Integrity:** Do this person's actions, decisions, dialogue, and reactions make sense given who the author has established them to be?

Our program needs to understand all three.

And importantly, **a flat character is not the same thing as a flat character arc.**

In K. M. Weiland's terminology, a Flat Arc character can be complex, fascinating, and fully developed. The character may already possess an important truth and influence the world around them rather than undergoing a conventional internal transformation.

That's very different from a one-dimensional character who exists only to serve the plot.

## 2. We need a comprehensive character model

I wouldn't want the system to judge character depth by how many biographical fields the author fills out.

Knowing someone's favorite food, birthday, and shoe size doesn't automatically make them interesting.

Instead, I'd organize character development around several dimensions.

| Dimension | What we examine |
|---|---|
| Identity | Background, culture, family, personal history, lived experiences |
| Personality | Temperament, habits, humor, quirks, strengths, weaknesses |
| Psychology | Fears, insecurities, emotional wounds, desires, beliefs |
| Values | What the character considers important and why |
| Motivation | What drives their choices, both consciously and unconsciously |
| Contradictions | Where their behavior, desires, and beliefs conflict |
| Relationships | How they behave differently with different people |
| Agency | Whether they make meaningful choices that influence events |
| Voice | Distinctive dialogue, vocabulary, thought patterns, humor |
| Behavior | How they respond to pressure, uncertainty, success, and failure |
| Character Arc | What changes, what remains constant, and why |

Notice that we're not simply collecting facts.

**We're building an understanding of how this person operates.**

And the author should be able to develop these dimensions gradually without completing an enormous questionnaire.

## 3. The feature I'd especially want: Character Integrity Checks

Your concern about characters making inexplicable decisions is particularly important.

Suppose you've established Kevin Wickley as someone who is suspicious, prideful, and extremely sensitive to perceived disrespect.

Then, in Scene 18, Kevin suddenly accepts Anthony's explanation without questioning him.

That might be completely appropriate.

But the program should examine whether the story has earned that change.

It might ask:

*Kevin has consistently interpreted Anthony's behavior as hostile. In Scene 18, he accepts Anthony's explanation without apparent hesitation. Has something happened to change Kevin's understanding, or is this reaction intentionally unusual?*

That's a useful observation.

But here's the critical distinction:

**Consistent characterization does not require predictable behavior.**

People behave inconsistently all the time.

A brave character can become frightened.

A selfish character can perform an unexpectedly generous act.

A reserved character can have an emotional outburst.

Those contradictions can make characters more believable, not less.

The question is whether the behavior has convincing psychological or situational foundations.

Our program should recognize the difference between **meaningful complexity and unsupported inconsistency**.

## 4. I want the program to understand character contradictions

This is where characters become interesting.

Imagine Anthony presents himself as completely unbothered by Kevin's antics.

But perhaps he's more sensitive to disrespect than he wants anyone to know.

That discrepancy could be fascinating.

His outward behavior says one thing.

His internal experience says another.

And his actions might reveal a third.

The program could track:

**Public identity:** Who the character wants others to believe they are.

**Private identity:** What the character believes about themselves.

**Demonstrated behavior:** What the character actually does.

**Underlying motivation:** What may be driving the discrepancy.

These layers would be optional development tools, not assumptions about Anthony that we've already established.

They would help authors create characters with recognizable psychological depth.

## 5. Character relationships should be dynamic

Another problem with conventional character profiles is that they describe people in isolation.

But characters reveal themselves through relationships.

Kevin might behave one way with Anthony, another with Francine, and another with someone whose opinion he deeply values.

That doesn't necessarily make him inconsistent.

It makes him human.

I'd want the system to track relationships as evolving dramatic entities.

For each significant relationship, it could examine trust, respect, intimacy, resentment, dependence, rivalry, and the balance of power.

And, more importantly, **what causes those relationships to change**.

The program could identify whether a reconciliation has sufficient groundwork or whether a betrayal is psychologically plausible given the relationship's history.

This connects directly to our causal integrity system.

## 6. We also need to track character agency

Here's another reason characters sometimes feel flat.

They don't actually influence the story.

Things happen to them, and they react, but their decisions rarely cause meaningful consequences.

Now, a character can be temporarily powerless. That's not inherently bad.

But I'd want the program to examine whether important characters have opportunities to exercise agency appropriate to their narrative roles.

For example, it might observe:

*Across the last six scenes, Anthony has primarily responded to Kevin's actions. His decisions have not yet produced a significant new consequence.*

That doesn't mean the author must immediately give Anthony a dramatic victory.

It simply raises a worthwhile question:

**Is Anthony actively shaping the conflict, or has he temporarily become a passenger in his own storyline?**

That's particularly relevant to your alternating-POV structure.

## 7. Character Voice Analysis

I think this could become one of the program's most useful features once there's an actual manuscript to examine.

Imagine selecting Kevin and Anthony and asking the application to compare their narrative voices.

Because both narrate in first person, their voices need to be distinguishable.

The program could examine patterns involving vocabulary, sentence rhythm, humor, observations, emotional language, and how each character interprets the same circumstances.

For example:

Kevin might describe an incident through suspicion and perceived disrespect.

Anthony might describe it through dry amusement and detached observation.

The software could identify places where their voices become unusually similar.

But again, it should frame the observation carefully.

Similar wording doesn't automatically mean poor characterization.

And the program should never require exaggerated dialect, stereotypes, or artificial speech patterns to distinguish characters.

**Voice should emerge from personality, perspective, and experience.**

## 8. Character Depth Diagnostics

Here's how I imagine the program helping an author who suspects a character is boring or underdeveloped.

Rather than declaring, "Your character lacks depth," it could examine several questions:

- Does the character demonstrate recognizable desires beyond their immediate plot function?
- Do their decisions reveal personal values?
- Are they capable of surprising the reader in believable ways?
- Do their relationships reveal different aspects of their personality?
- Do their actions produce consequences?
- Does the character have meaningful strengths as well as weaknesses?
- Are important behavioral changes adequately motivated?
- Is there a distinction between what they say, think, want, and do?

And I would be particularly careful with supporting characters.

**Not every character requires the same level of development.**

A neighbor who appears twice doesn't need the psychological complexity of Kevin, Anthony, or Francine.

The system should evaluate characters relative to their narrative importance.

Otherwise, we'd create another planning trap where an author feels compelled to develop forty-page biographies for every character who walks into a scene!

Naturally, this belongs within Narrative Zoom.

Imagine selecting Kevin Wickley.

You could see his character profile, beliefs, values, contradictions, relationships, and development throughout the novel.

That would help you identify whether the transformation feels earned.

That's where Character Integrity Analysis and Causal Integrity Analysis become interconnected.

You recently established that Kevin, Anthony, and Francine are African American characters living in a racially diverse neighborhood.

That's an established part of your storyworld.

But we shouldn't assume that shared racial identity means shared personalities, beliefs, experiences, cultural expressions, or speech patterns.

Each character should be developed as an individual.

The program should preserve the identities you've established while avoiding unsupported assumptions about how characters should behave because of their demographic characteristics.

That principle should apply across cultures, religions, ages, socioeconomic backgrounds, and other aspects of identity.

When specialized research would genuinely help, our Craft Resource Advisor could recommend relevant materials.

**The program must never confuse an incomplete character profile with an incomplete character.**

You might know exactly how Francine thinks without having decided where she went to college.

You might understand Kevin's fears without knowing his birthday.

And some aspects of Anthony's personality may only become clear when you begin writing his dialogue.

That's normal.

We should allow the author to discover the character through writing.

The application can help identify unanswered questions, but it shouldn't demand answers merely to fill empty fields.

**YES! And I'm glad you brought us back to McKee because I think his concept of THE GAP should be central to the intelligence of our program.**

And you're absolutely right to distinguish the gap in a character's behavior from the larger dramatic gap McKee discusses in *Story*.

They're related, but they aren't the same thing.

## 1. McKee's Gap Between Expectation and Result

One of McKee's most important ideas concerns the difference between **what a character expects to happen when they take an action and what actually happens.**

A character wants something.

They take an action they believe will produce the desired result.

But the world responds differently than expected.

**That difference is the gap.**

And that gap creates new circumstances, forces the character to respond, and can generate progressively greater conflict.

Consider *I Declare War*.

Imagine Kevin decides to humiliate Anthony with a prank.

**Desire:** Kevin wants to regain his dignity and establish superiority.

**Expectation:** Anthony will be embarrassed, and Kevin will finally have the upper hand.

**Action:** Kevin executes his plan.

**Actual result:** Anthony finds the entire thing hilarious and retaliates in a way Kevin never anticipated.

**THE GAP:** Kevin expected victory but instead experiences greater humiliation.

Now Kevin has a new problem.

He must respond to circumstances he didn't anticipate.

And his response creates another opportunity for things to go wrong.

That's the dramatic engine McKee is describing.

## 2. The Gap Should Be Tracked at Multiple Levels

Here's where I think our software can do something particularly useful.

We shouldn't limit gap analysis to individual scenes.

| Narrative level | What the program examines |
|---|---|
| **Character** | The difference between self-perception, stated values, and demonstrated behavior |
| **Scene** | The gap between intended outcome and actual result |
| **Sequence** | How successive gaps create complications and increasingly difficult choices |
| **Act** | How the accumulated consequences produce a major reversal |
| **Story** | How the protagonist's pursuit of a desire ultimately exposes a deeper need or truth |

These are different analytical applications of McKee's principles, not identical definitions of his scene-level gap.

And I particularly want the software to understand that distinction.

## 3. Progressive Complications Are Essential

This is another McKee concept we should incorporate deeply.

**An effective dramatic progression doesn't merely repeat conflict. It changes the nature, intensity, or consequences of the conflict.**

Imagine Kevin attempts three different pranks.

All three fail.

But each failure produces essentially the same result.

That might give us three funny scenes, but we may not have meaningful progressive complications.

Now imagine:

The first prank fails and embarrasses Kevin.

The second makes Anthony suspicious and damages Kevin's reputation.

The third exposes a vulnerability Kevin has spent years concealing.

Now the conflict is becoming more personal.

The stakes are evolving.

And the character is being forced into increasingly difficult circumstances.

Our program should be able to examine that progression.

It might ask:

*These three scenes each involve unsuccessful retaliation. However, the consequences appear similar. Does each failure meaningfully increase the pressure, change the relationship, or create a new obstacle?*

That's a much more sophisticated question than simply asking whether the stakes increase.

## 4. We Need to Incorporate McKee's Forces of Antagonism

I also want this to become a major analytical feature.

McKee's discussion of antagonism goes beyond identifying a villain.

The protagonist encounters resistance through different kinds of forces, including internal conflict, personal relationships, and broader external circumstances.

In *I Declare War*, Kevin isn't simply fighting Anthony.

He's also fighting his own paranoia, pride, and need for validation.

And, unbeknownst to him, he's fighting Francine's strategic manipulation.

The strongest conflict can emerge when those forces reinforce one another.

For example, Francine's manipulation works partly because Kevin's paranoia makes him susceptible to misinterpreting events.

**The external antagonist exploits the protagonist's internal weakness.**

That's an important relationship for our program to recognize.

And it ties directly into your concern about believable, well-developed characters.

## 5. Another McKee Principle: The Value at Stake

We already discussed positive-to-negative and negative-to-positive scene values.

But I want to make sure our analysis goes deeper than attaching a plus or minus symbol to every scene.

For example:

**Scene value:** Respect

**Opening condition:** Kevin believes he has regained Anthony's respect.

**Closing condition:** Kevin is publicly humiliated.

That's a clear reversal.

But we should also ask:

**What caused the reversal?**

**What expectation was violated?**

**What does Kevin do because of the reversal?**

**Does the resulting decision create the next meaningful conflict?**

This connects four things we've discussed:

**Story Value → Expectation/Result Gap → Character Response → Causal Consequence**

That's a powerful analytical chain.

And I think it deserves to become one of the central mechanisms in our scene-analysis system.

## 6. I Want to Add One More McKee Concept: The Negation of the Negation

This is where his treatment of story values becomes particularly interesting.

McKee discusses how conflict can push beyond a simple positive-versus-negative opposition into more extreme conditions.

Consider the value of justice.

Its opposite is injustice.

But a more extreme condition might involve institutionalized injustice or the deliberate corruption of justice itself.

For *I Declare War*, we could explore a similar progression around respect.

A possible value scale might be:

**Respect → Disrespect → Humiliation → Dehumanization**

That's an illustrative scale, not one you've committed to for the novel.

And I wouldn't necessarily push your comedy into that final territory.

But understanding the spectrum helps us distinguish ordinary conflict from increasingly serious consequences.

The software could let authors define their own value scales and examine where scenes fall along them.

This would be especially useful when you move into psychological thrillers or horror, where the negative end of a value scale can become considerably darker.

## 7. Here's the feature I'd add to Phase 2

### The Dramatic Gap & Progressive Complications Analyzer

This would work alongside Character Depth & Integrity Analysis and Causal Integrity Analysis.

For each relevant scene, it would examine:

1. **Desire:** What does the character want?
2. **Expectation:** What result does the character anticipate?
3. **Action:** What does the character actually do?
4. **Opposition:** What forces resist that action?
5. **Actual result:** What happens instead?
6. **The gap:** How does reality differ from expectation?
7. **Value change:** What meaningful condition changes?
8. **Response:** How does the character react to the unexpected result?
9. **New choice:** What decision follows?
10. **Progressive complication:** How does that choice create greater or different dramatic pressure?

Not every scene would need all ten fields completed. Some might contain multiple action-and-gap cycles.

And the program should distinguish between information explicitly established by the author, information observed in the manuscript, and interpretive suggestions.

### The most important part

**The analyzer should investigate the gap between intention and outcome, not manufacture unexpected outcomes just to satisfy a formula.**

A character can achieve exactly what they intended and still create an unforeseen consequence.

A successful action might produce a devastating result elsewhere.

And a quiet scene may contain a subtle but consequential shift rather than an explosive reversal.

We must preserve that sophistication.

## 8. And this belongs in Narrative Zoom!

Imagine opening a scene and seeing:

**Kevin's expectation:** Anthony will finally back down.

**Actual result:** Anthony doubles down.

**Gap:** Kevin's attempt to assert control produces greater disrespect.

**Value change:** Apparent superiority → Humiliation.

**New decision:** Kevin escalates.

**Causal dependency:** His escalation triggers the next sequence.

Now zoom out.

You can see how this scene-level gap contributes to the entire sequence's reversal.

Zoom out again.

You can see how the sequence contributes to the act-level turning point.

**That's exactly the relationship between the big picture and the intricacies that you've been describing.**

And importantly, the program could identify when a scene's outcome doesn't convincingly create the next action.

We're bringing McKee's dramatic principles together with the causal integrity analysis you were so excited about.

I would want McKee to be one of our **primary analytical lenses**, alongside Snyder, Weiland, and Ingermanson.

But I wouldn't want the application simply to reproduce his terminology and ask authors to fill in forms.

I want it to understand the dramatic relationships those concepts describe.

Because you could have every scene labeled correctly and still end up with a story that doesn't work.

**The labels aren't the story. The dramatic movement is.**

And that's what I want our program to help you see.

Your objective isn't to prove that you've followed McKee correctly.

It's to write compelling scenes populated by believable characters whose choices create meaningful consequences.

And then connect those scenes into a novel that readers don't want to put down.

**That's what we're building toward.**

**Idea:** What if Kevin accidentally becomes famous in the neighborhood for something utterly humiliating?

**Idea:** What if something Anthony considers insignificant turns out to mean a great deal to Francine?

**Idea:** What if there's an ongoing neighborhood joke that pays off spectacularly in Act III?

These are illustrative possibilities, not new decisions about your novel.

You can collect them without committing to any of them.

And the system should never automatically promote an idea into established story canon.

### Here's the feature I'd add: Explore Without Committing

You select an idea and ask:

**"What would this change?"**

The system could examine its possible effects on characterization, plot, relationships, pacing, and causality.

Or you could ask:

**"Where might this fit?"**

It might suggest a sequence, scene, or dramatic turning point where the idea could be useful.

But nothing changes in your actual story until you decide.

That's how we preserve your creative freedom.

---

## 3. The really exciting part: Questions and ideas can connect!

Imagine this:

Under **Questions I Have**, you've written:

*How can I make the midpoint more surprising?*

Meanwhile, three weeks earlier, under **Things & Ideas I'm Thinking About**, you captured:

*What if someone witnesses something important but completely misunderstands what they're seeing?*

The application recognizes a possible connection.

It brings that earlier idea to your attention when you're examining the midpoint.

**You don't have to remember that you had the idea.**

That's precisely the kind of cognitive load we want the Story Brain to take off your shoulders.

And if the connection doesn't interest you?

Dismiss it.

The original thought remains safely stored.

---

## 4. And here's something else I want: Questions that generate more questions

Because that's often how genuine story development works.

You answer one question and realize it creates three others.

Instead of scattering them across separate notes, the program could preserve their relationships.

For example:

**Original question:** Why does Kevin distrust Anthony?

**Possible answer:** Kevin misinterpreted something Anthony did.

**New questions:**
- What did Anthony actually do?
- Why did Kevin interpret it incorrectly?
- When does the reader discover the truth?
- Does Anthony know Kevin misunderstood him?

The original question becomes the starting point of a connected exploration.

And all of it can remain linked to the relevant characters and scenes.

No more losing the thread.

---

## 5. One design decision I feel strongly about

I do **not** want these sections to become two enormous lists you have to scroll through.

You should be able to capture something in either section and forget about organizing it.

Later, the application could surface relevant entries based on what you're working on.

It should also let you see everything when you want to review your thoughts.

And each entry should have a simple status, without requiring a complicated workflow.

For questions: **Open, Answered, or No Longer Relevant.**

For ideas: **Considering, Adopted, or Set Aside.**

Importantly, *Set Aside* doesn't mean deleted.

An idea you don't use in *I Declare War* might become perfect for another novel.

And an unanswered question isn't necessarily a writing blocker.

---

## 6. I'd put both sections somewhere very easy to reach

Not buried inside a menu.

Not hidden in a character profile.

Not requiring you to navigate away from your manuscript.

I'd want a quick-capture button accessible throughout the program:

**+ Capture a Thought**

Then you choose:

**Question I Have** or **Idea I'm Thinking About**.

You can enter a sentence, several paragraphs, or an unpolished brain dump.

And return to whatever you were doing.

If you haven't decided which category something belongs to, the program can simply save it as a thought and let you decide later.

No compulsory categorization.

No interruption to your creative momentum.

---

### There's one last feature I think you'll appreciate.

**"What was I thinking about?"**

Imagine opening *I Declare War* after being away for two weeks.

Instead of searching through your notebooks, you can ask the application that question.

It could show you the last questions you were exploring, the ideas you were considering, and the connections you were investigating.

You could pick up your thinking without having to reconstruct it.

And then, crucially, return to writing.

### So our Story Brain now has two dedicated spaces:

**QUESTIONS I HAVE**  
*The things I need, want, or might eventually need to figure out.*

**THINGS & IDEAS I'M THINKING ABOUT**  
*The possibilities, inspirations, experiments, and random flashes that might become something wonderful.*

Both connect to the story. Neither requires immediate action. Neither gets lost.

And neither is allowed to turn into another elaborate administrative system.

**Because the whole point is to stop making your brain serve as the storage device for your imagination.**

## 1. First, there's a factual error in the Fish-Guts Sequence poster

This is the most important correction.

Your story bible establishes that **Miss Francine dumps the fish guts into Anthony's yard while Kevin and Anthony are distracted by the five-dollar bill.**

Anthony subsequently blames Kevin, who truthfully denies responsibility.

But the generated companion poster depicts **Kevin as the person who dumps the fish guts**.

That's incorrect.

It changes the entire causal structure of the sequence!

The actual chain is:

**Francine plants the five-dollar bill → Kevin becomes suspicious → Anthony picks it up to irritate Kevin → Francine uses their distraction to dump the fish guts → The smell and animals eventually expose the problem → Anthony blames Kevin → Kevin denies it → Their conflict escalates.**

And remember, the animals don't arrive immediately. That delay is part of the established sequence.

This is a perfect example of why our **Causal Integrity Analyzer** matters.

The poster looks wonderful, but its explanation changes who did what, why, and what happens next.

That must be corrected before printing.

## 2. Our recent discussions suggest five improvements

|---|---|
| **Character Depth & Integrity** | Add character motivations, contradictions, behavioral consistency, and decision-making pressure. |
| **McKee's Dramatic Gap** | Show what characters expect, what actually happens, and how the difference drives the next action. |
| **Progressive Complications** | Distinguish escalating dramatic consequences from a simple series of increasingly outrageous pranks. |
| **Questions I Have** | Identify unresolved story questions without treating them as structural failures. |
| **Ideas I'm Thinking About** | Distinguish possibilities you're exploring from decisions you've actually made. |

These additions would make the companion posters substantially more useful.

Ahhhh! **That's an important distinction, and it changes how we should represent that sequence.**

The **distraction is the concept. The five-dollar bill is one possible execution of it.**

So here's how I would classify the elements:

| Story element | Status |
|---|---|
| Francine secretly orchestrates the fish-guts incident | **Established** |
| Kevin and Anthony are distracted, giving Francine an opportunity | **Established concept** |
| A five-dollar bill serves as the distraction | **Possible execution, not decided** |
| Francine dumps fish guts into Anthony's yard | **Established** |
| Anthony suspects Kevin | **Established** |
| Kevin truthfully denies responsibility | **Established** |
| The smell and subsequent animal activity escalate the situation | **Established** |
| Exact distraction mechanics and scene choreography | **Still developing** |

### And this illustrates something critical about our Story Brain.

**A story decision can be established at one level while its execution remains undecided.**

That's different from marking the entire scene either *decided* or *undecided*.

For example:

**Scene objective:** Create an opportunity for Francine to sabotage Anthony's yard without being observed.

**Established mechanism:** Both men become distracted.

**Possible execution:** The five-dollar bill.

**Unresolved question:** What distraction would be funniest, most believable, and most consistent with Kevin's and Anthony's personalities?

That's precisely the kind of distinction our software must preserve.

And here's another McKee connection: we can explore different distractions by examining how each creates an expectation, produces a gap, and affects the resulting action.

We should be able to compare possibilities **without silently turning any of them into canon**.

### What this means for the Fish-Guts poster

Rather than showing a five-dollar bill as a confirmed plot point, the revised poster should say:

**FRANCINE'S DISTRACTION**

*The men become occupied with something that gives Francine the opportunity to execute her plan.*

**Execution: UNDECIDED**

*Five-dollar bill is one possibility.*

That keeps the story's causal architecture intact while leaving you complete creative freedom to find the best version.

And I want to incorporate one additional principle into Phase 2:

**Decisions have layers. A confirmed story function does not automatically confirm the specific events used to accomplish it.**

This will matter enormously when we build your Questions I Have and Things & Ideas I'm Thinking About sections.

Thank you for catching that distinction. It's exactly why reviewing these visualizations is proving so useful.

**We're not just mapping your novel. We're learning how to preserve the difference between what you know about your story and what you're still discovering.**

We need to turn the *I Declare War* posters from **beautiful AI-generated illustrations into professionally produced, fact-checked publishing files**.

And we already have most of the ingredients. We have your story bible, the visual designs you love, and the decisions we've made throughout our conversations.

What we need now is a proper production process.

## Phase 1: Getting your posters ready for printing

I'd divide the remaining work into five stages.

### 1. Establish the story bible as our source of truth

First, we need to review each poster against your October 13, 2026 story bible.

Every statement on a poster should fall into one of four categories:

| Classification | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Established** | You've made this creative decision. |
| **Developing** | You're exploring possibilities but haven't decided. |
| **Unanswered** | You've identified something you still need to figure out. |
| **Illustrative** | An example we've created to demonstrate a storytelling principle, not an actual story decision. |

This will prevent us from accidentally inventing character motivations, scene events, or plot developments.

For example, the fish-guts incident would retain Francine as the perpetrator while leaving the distraction's specific execution undecided.

**Deliverable:** A verified master story-data file from which every poster draws its information.

### 2. Correct the structure and narrative details

Next, we'd reconcile all ten planned posters with that master file.

This includes verifying the Save the Cat beats, approximate percentages and page calculations, McKee's dramatic principles, character relationships, alternating POVs, and the ledger's discovery and eventual use.

We also need to preserve a particularly important distinction: a story event can be established even when the specific way it happens remains undecided.

**Deliverable:** A content-approved specification for each poster.

### 3. Rebuild the posters as editable designs

This is the most significant technical step.

Rather than asking an image generator to reproduce paragraphs and tiny numbers, we'd use actual typography, vector diagrams, and precisely positioned elements.

We can retain the illustrated neighborhood scenes, portraits, flowers, and purple-and-gold visual identity you love.

But the text, arrows, timelines, labels, and tables should become independent design elements.

That gives us three advantages: perfect spelling and numerical accuracy, sharp text at any printing size, and the ability to revise individual details later.

**Deliverable:** Editable master designs and print-quality PDFs.

### 4. Prepare the printing editions

I recommend producing three distinct editions, not simply resizing one image.

| Edition | Dimensions | Intended use |
|---|---|---|
| **Large wall poster** | 48 × 36 inches | Your primary story-planning wall |
| **Extra-large wall poster** | 60 × 45 inches | Maximum visibility and detailed study |
| **Desk reference** | 8.5 × 11 inches | Reviewing the story at your desk |

The two wall posters can share the same vector-based design because they have identical proportions.

The desk editions should be reformatted for legibility. Some particularly dense posters may need two or more pages rather than squeezing everything onto one sheet.

For printed illustrations, we'd ensure appropriate image resolution at the final size. Vector text and diagrams will remain sharp independently of those images.

**Deliverable:** Press-ready PDFs with correctly sized pages and appropriate print settings.

### 5. Perform a final quality-control inspection

Before approving anything, we'd check every poster at its intended printing dimensions.

That means checking actual text legibility, page numbers, arrows, diagram connections, margins, and image sharpness.

I'd also verify that revisions haven't introduced new story inaccuracies.

The last step would be a printable proof, ideally at actual size for a portion containing the smallest text.

**Deliverable:** A final approved printing package.

## What happens to the ten posters?

We'll keep the collection we discussed:

**Three master maps:** Chronological Story Map, Narrative Relationship Map, and Story Command Center.

**Five existing companion maps:** Act I, Act IIA, Act IIB, Act III, and the Fish-Guts Sequence.

**Two new companions:** Character Depth & Integrity and McKee's Dramatic Engine.

**I don't want to generate all ten again and hope they're correct.**

That's what created some of our problems.

Instead, I'd establish the verified content and develop one finished production-quality poster as our standard.

My choice would be the **Chronological Story Map**.

This will also let us preserve the look you love without repeatedly introducing errors through image generation.

We already have the October 13 story bible and your design preferences.

The posters should accurately reflect **the story as it exists today**, including the unanswered questions.

That's their job.

**Every finished poster must pass three tests:**

**1. Story integrity:** Is every statement faithful to your established decisions, with possibilities clearly distinguished?

**2. Visual integrity:** Are the information hierarchy, relationships, and diagrams clear and meaningful?

**3. Print integrity:** Can the file be printed at its intended dimensions with sharp text, suitable illustrations, and readable details?

**Does this poster make it easier for you to understand your story and get back to writing?**

Because that is the entire reason we're doing this.

**First, we build the verified story-data foundation. Then we produce the Chronological Story Map as our first fully print-ready master.**

That gives us a dependable foundation for every companion poster and, eventually, the Story Brain application.

And once we've completed that process, you'll have something considerably more valuable than enlarged AI artwork.

You'll have a **coordinated, editable, accurate visual storytelling system** that you can put on your wall, reference while writing, and update as *I Declare War* develops.

That's the standard I want us to meet before you spend a dime at the printer.

# PDF Skill (Read • Inspect • Extract • Edit • Render • Forms • OCR • Redact • Convert • Diff)

This skill is designed for **reliable, workflow-driven** PDF work: **render -> verify -> operate -> re-render verify**.

## Before you touch PDFs: should this be DOCX/PPTX instead?

Even if the user asks for a PDF deliverable, the best workflow is often:

- **Text-heavy, business-doc layout (headings, TOC, long tables, rich lists)** -> use the **DOCX skill** to author, then convert to PDF with `lo_convert_to_pdf.py`.
- **Slide-like visual layout (charts, callouts, fixed positioning, figure captions)** -> use the **Slides skill** (PPTX) to author, then export to PDF.
- **Programmatic generation** -> ReportLab (this skill) is fine.

If you find yourself hand-tuning line breaks or typography in ReportLab, you probably picked the wrong authoring format.

## Design standards for document generation

For generating new documents or major rewrite/repackages, follow the design standards below unless the user explicitly requests otherwise. The user's instructions always take precedence; otherwise, adhere to these standards.

When creating the document design, do not compromise on the content and make factual/technical errors. Do not produce something that looks polished but not actually what the user requested.

It is very important that the document is professional and aesthetically pleasing. As such, you should follow this general workflow to make your final delivered document:

1. Before you make the PDF, please first think about the high-level design of the PDF:
   - Before creating the document, decide what kind of document it is (for example, a memo, report, SOP, workflow, form, proposal, or manual) and design accordingly. In general, you shall create documents which are professional, visually polished, and aesthetically pleasing. However, you should also calibrate the level of styling to the document's purpose: for formal, serious, or highly utilitarian documents, visual appeal should come mainly from strong typography, spacing, hierarchy, and overall polish rather than expressive styling. The goal is for the document's visual character to feel appropriate to its real-world use case, with readability and usability always taking priority.
   - You should make documents that feel visually natural. If a human looks at your document, they should find the design natural and smooth. This is very important; please think carefully about how to achieve this.
   - Think about how you would like the first page to be organized. How about subsequent pages? What about the placement of the title? What does the heading ladder look like? Should there be a clear hierarchy? etc
   - Would you like to include visual components, such as tables, callouts, checklists, images, etc? If yes, then plan out the design for each component.
   - Think about the general spacing and layout. What will be the default body spacing? What page budget is allocated between packaging and substance? How will page breaks behave around tables and figures, since we must make sure to avoid large blank gaps, keep captions and their visuals together when possible, and keep content from becoming too wide by maintaining generous side margins so the page feels balanced and natural.
   - Think about font, type scale, consistent accent treatment, etc. Try to avoid forcing large chunks of small text into narrow areas. When space is tight, adjust font size, line breaks, alignment, or layout instead of cramming in more text.
2. Once you have a working PDF, continue iterating until the entire document is polished and correct. After every change or edit, render the PDF and review it carefully to evaluate the result. The plan from (1) should guide you, but it is only a flexible draft; you should update your decisions as needed throughout the revision process. Important: each time you render and reflect, you should check for both:
   1. Design aesthetics: the document should be aesthetically pleasing and easy to skim. Ask yourself: if a human were to look at my document, would they find it aesthetically nice? It should feel natural, smooth, and visually cohesive.
   2. Formatting issues that need to be fixed: e.g. text overlap, overflow, cramped spacing between adjacent elements, awkward spacing in tables/charts, awkward page breaks, etc. This is super important. Do not stop revising until all formatting issues are fixed.

While making and revising the PDF, please adhere to and check against these quality reminders, to ensure the deliverable is visually high quality:

- Document density: Try to avoid having verbose dense walls of text, unless it's necessary. Avoid long runs of consecutive plain paragraphs or too many words before visual anchors. For some tasks this may be necessary (i.e. verbose legal documents); in those cases ignore this suggestion.
- Font: Use professional, easy-to-read font choices with appropriate size that is not too small. Usage of bold, underlines, and italics should be professional.
- Color: Use color intentionally for titles, headings, subheadings, and selective emphasis so important information stands out in a visually appealing way. The palette and intensity should fit the document's purpose, with more restrained use where a formal or serious tone is needed.

  - Suggestions:
    - Set deliberate table/cell widths and heights instead of defaulting to full page width.
    - Choose column widths intentionally rather than giving every column equal width by default. Very short fields (for example: item number, checkbox, score, result, year, date, or status) should usually be kept compact, while wider columns should be reserved for longer content.
    - Avoid overly wide tables, and leave generous side margins so the layout feels natural.
    - Keep all text vertically centered and make deliberate horizontal alignment choices.

      - Never use fixed row heights that can truncate text; allow rows to expand with wrapped content.
      - Ensure cell padding and line spacing are sufficient so descenders/ascenders don't get clipped.
      - If content is tight, prefer (in order): wrap text -> adjust column widths -> reduce font slightly -> abbreviate headers/use two-line headers.
